subject: Science
title: Test rock hardness and water
objective_verbatim: Test rocks for hardness and whether they let water through.
reading_age_est: rough ARI grade 1.9 on 669 pupil-visible words; heuristic age guide 7.9 years, not a formal reading-age test
pupil_words: I am learning to test a rock in two ways.
success_criteria: I can show a safe mark test.
I can watch where drops go.
I can tell what I saw.

vocab.definition: how hard a thing is to mark
a liquid used in our test

retrieval.question: How can we sort two rocks?
retrieval.answer: Check a property you can see or feel.

retrieval.question: What can we do with a clean tub?
Name one body part that helps protect organs.

stages.adult_text: Offer a safe kit choice and short first–then cue.

stages.pupil_text: Think back. Say, sign or point.
stages.adult_text: Ask three low-stakes prior questions; answers in note.
Pre-teach words; show the full model; ask the show-me check.
Hand over the missing step; offer F or H route. Reset once.

stages.pupil_text: All of us show one choice.
stages.adult_text: Take all pupil responses at once; use decision rule and parallel hinge.

stages.pupil_text: Show each test. Record what you saw.
stages.adult_text: Choose one adult for supported pupils, one for group; swap across the week.

stages.pupil_text: Check one result. Hear a next step.
stages.adult_text: Give VF and one NS(+); invite one self-edit. Reset once.

stages.pupil_text: Tell an adult what you saw.
stages.adult_text: Hear feedback and next step, choose next start, then one-minute reset.

worked_example.full: Adult uses one blunt tool. A gets a mark. Three drops stay on top.
worked_example.faded: Mark B. Add three drops. The drops ____.
worked_example.removed_step: State the observed result at rock B, rather than guess it.
worked_example.fade_next: Pupil picks the test step and result from the unlabelled kit.

cfu.question: Is a wet top proof that water went right through?
cfu.answer: No. Look beneath the rock or in the tray to check whether any water passed through.

hinge.question: The tray under a new rock C is wet before the water test. What should the class do first?

options.text: Call C porous from the wet tray.
options.diagnosis: Uses water present before the test as a result.

options.text: Call C hard from the wet tray.
options.diagnosis: Confuses a water clue with hardness.

options.text: Skip the test and guess from colour.
options.diagnosis: Uses appearance instead of the planned check.

options.text: Dry the tray, then repeat the test.
options.diagnosis: Removes the old water before observing a new result.

hinge.decision_rule: About 3 in 4 or more right → move on; otherwise re-model Adult uses one blunt tool. A gets a mark. Three drops stay on top. Ask the parallel hinge. No scores or answers saved.
hinge.parallel_hinge: A drop from new rock D runs around its edge into a dry tray. Does that prove water passed through D? No; check the route and repeat safely.

misconceptions.misconception: A wet surface proves water went through a rock.
misconceptions.spot: Points to a wet top as the result.
misconceptions.correction: Check the underside and tray; state only what was observed.

misconceptions.misconception: The scratch test and water test measure the same thing.
misconceptions.spot: Uses scratch result to answer a water question.
misconceptions.correction: Compare two separate result columns, mark and water through.

we_do.support: Watch one drop. Point to the top or tray.
we_do.stretch: Why must each rock get the same drops?

tiers.F: Point to a mark and a wet rock.
tiers.M: Show both tests. Tell what you saw.
tiers.H: Why use the same tool and drops?

stems.F: I can see ____ on the rock.
stems.H: This is fair as I kept ____ the same.

tiers.go_deeper: Could a hard rock also let water through? Use each test result.
tiers.early_finisher: A drop slides off. How will you fix the test?

adaptations.cognition_learning: Give a three-step visual card for test rock hardness and water; remove its last cue after a correct try.
adaptations.communication_interaction: Point to the real kit before a short spoken, signed or AAC response; wait for a turn.
adaptations.semh: Offer a private first–then cue and planned pause before the hinge; re-enter with one step.
adaptations.sensory_physical: Use a stable tray, large cards or an accessible input; no forced touch.
adaptations.eal: Rehearse a full M or H idea in any language before writing; keep the science challenge.

speaking_frames: This is fair as I kept ____ the same.

ta_focus.i_do: Watch my first step. What do you see?
ta_focus.we_do: What step is missing? Show it with the kit.
ta_focus.independent: What can you do first on your own?

prompt_ladder: Point to the object or model.
Ask: What will you check next?
Model one step and give the next turn back.
Finish one example together, then let the pupil try.

F.q: Point to the tray below the rock.
F.a: The tray that catches drops beneath it.

M.q: Does a wet top prove water went through?
M.a: No. Check beneath the rock and tray.

H.q: Why use the same tool and drops?
H.a: Then the rock is the planned change in the check.

H.q: What does a drawing leave out?
H.a: It cannot show whether drops truly passed through a sample.

diagrams.alt: Three cutaway models with droppers and trays: drops remain on top; drops pass through pores; or drops run round a rock edge. Inspect the real route.
diagrams.caption: Check the path: on top, through the rock or round its edge. The pictures are models, not test results. Simplified; not to scale.

method: Adult tests a mark on each rock.
Add three drops to A. Check the edge and below.
Do the same on B. Record the route seen.
practical.risk: Check against the school risk assessment and CLEAPSS guidance. Adult handles tool, inspects edges and controls water; no dust or tasting.
practical.pupil_risk: Tools or rough rocks may hurt skin; spills may be slippery.
practical.pupil_safety: Let staff use the tool. Keep drops in the tray. Do not taste; wash hands after.

facts.claim: Rocks differ in hardness and water movement; a simple check can compare samples.
A wet top alone does not show water moved through the rock; passage through must be observed.
Water moves through connected spaces in some porous and permeable rocks.
In this authored open-tray setup, drops seen below may have run round the edge; staff must inspect the actual route before claiming passage through.
facts.source: Authored classroom apparatus; inspect actual route during lesson

facts.claim: A visible mark from the same blunt tool is one classroom comparison of surface response, not a formal hardness scale.
Vocabulary term hardness means how hard a thing is to mark; example: The tool marks this rock.
Vocabulary term absorb means take in a liquid; example: Water soaks in.
Vocabulary term water means a liquid used in our test; example: I add three drops.
Vocabulary term test means a check to find out; example: I test two rocks.
Retrieval question from SoW C40: How can we sort two rocks? Answer: Check a property you can see or feel.
Retrieval question from SoW C39: What can we do with a clean tub? Answer: Use it again if safe.
Retrieval question from SoW C32: Name one body part that helps protect organs. Answer: A skeleton or bones.
The “Through” route crosses the rock body, unlike a path around its edge; a real test needs a direct observation of that route.
The “On top” drop is not evidence that it passed through the rock.
The “Edge route” is an alternative route in this simplified classroom set-up; check actual apparatus before drawing a conclusion.
facts.source: Authored classroom apparatus; inspect actual route during lesson

regulation_line: Agree a quiet pause and supervised place. Give one short cue. Re-enter at the last completed step. No evidence while distressed.
